title: WNBA commissioner Cathy Engelbert retiring at end of 2026
content:
Cathy Engelbert’s tenure as commissioner of the WNBA is ending.

Engelbert, 61, released a statement through the league on Friday morning announcing that she will be stepping down at the end of 2026, finishing off a seven-year tenure that saw the league reach new heights of popularity and financial success but was also marked by withering criticism from players of her leadership.

“Over the years, it has been amazing to watch WNBA players thrive and lead the massive cultural surge around women’s sports,” Engelbert said in her statement. “I retire knowing we have built something bigger, stronger and more enduring than we could have imagined. I am grateful to the WNBA and NBA team owners and staff, players, investors, fans and the powerhouse league office staff, who believed in what this league could become. I retire with immense gratitude and tremendous optimism for the future of the WNBA, with the best yet to come.”

Engelbert, who was appointed as the WNBA’s first commissioner in 2019 after serving as the CEO of Deloitte, brokered two collective bargaining agreements, successfully navigated a pandemic season, and helped the league with plans to expand to 18 teams by 2030. The financial gains under her leadership have been unprecedented. She facilitated a $75 million capital raise that was initially viewed as a stabilizing move for the league but has since raised questions about the long-term implications of further convoluting the league’s ownership structure.

In 2024, the WNBA secured an 11-year media rights deal, which is now worth a reported $3 billion, but the credit for that has largely gone to the NBA and commissioner Adam Silver, who negotiated both leagues’ deals in tandem.

Engelbert has faced criticism from players for her overall leadership style, specifically from players who were outspoken about her lack of personal connection with them. Ultimately, Engelbert oversaw the ratification of a historic CBA, leading to player salaries that surpassed $1 million for the first time, and a groundbreaking revenue-sharing model that ties players’ salaries to revenue in a meaningful way.

NBA commissioner Adam Silver praised Engelbert in a statement released by the WNBA. “Cathy has presided over the WNBA through the most significant period of growth in the league’s 30-year history,” Silver said. “We are grateful for Cathy’s leadership and unwavering commitment to the advancement of women’s basketball.”

This story will be updated.
